items.stem: Which of the following is water in its solid state?

explain.why: A raindrop is liquid water.
A puddle is liquid water.
Water vapour is the gas state.

solution: A hailstone is a lump of ice, which is solid water.

items.stem: Which statement about water in the gas state is correct?
options: It has a fixed shape and can be seen easily
It can be seen and has a fixed volume always
It has a fixed shape and a fixed volume
It cannot be seen and has no fixed shape

explain.why: Water vapour is invisible and has no shape of its own.
Water vapour cannot be seen and it spreads out.
That describes a solid, such as ice.

solution: Water vapour is invisible and spreads out to fill the space it is in.

items.stem: Which state of water keeps its own shape?
options: Both liquid water and water vapour

explain.why: Liquid water takes the shape of its container.
Water vapour spreads out in any space.
Neither of these keeps its own shape.

solution: Only the solid state, ice, has a fixed shape.

items.stem: Which state of water takes the shape of its container but keeps the same volume?

explain.why: Ice keeps its own shape.
Water vapour also changes its volume to fill the space.
Ice does not take the shape of its container.

solution: A liquid can flow into the shape of a container, and its volume stays the same.

items.stem: Which letter in the diagram shows ice changing into water?

explain.why: Q is water changing into ice, which is freezing.
R is water changing into water vapour.
S is water vapour changing into water.

solution: Ice to water is melting, which is P.

explain.why: P is melting.
Q is freezing.
R is water changing into a gas, the opposite of condensation.

solution: Condensation is water vapour changing into liquid water, which is S.

items.stem: What is the change from liquid water to ice called?

explain.why: Melting is ice changing into water.
Boiling is water changing into a gas.
Condensation is a gas changing into a liquid.

solution: Liquid water changes to ice when it freezes.

items.stem: What is the change from water vapour to liquid water called?

explain.why: Evaporation is liquid water changing into water vapour.
Freezing is water changing into ice.
Melting is ice changing into water.

solution: A gas changing to a liquid is condensation.

items.stem: At which temperature does pure ice melt?

explain.why: 100 °C is the boiling point of water.
37 °C is the temperature of a healthy body.
Ice that is already melting is not this cold.

solution: Ice melts at 0 °C.

items.stem: At which temperature does pure water boil at sea level?

explain.why: 0 °C is the melting point of ice.
Water is not boiling yet at 90 °C.
This is a cold temperature.

solution: Water boils at 100 °C.

items.stem: Ice cubes on a plate in a warm room turn into water. What happens to the ice?

explain.why: Melting needs heat to be gained.
Freezing is the change from water to ice.
The ice is turning into water, not the other way round.

solution: The ice takes in heat from the warm room and melts.

items.stem: Droplets of water form on the outside of a glass of iced water. Where does the water come from?
options: Water that leaks through the glass
Ice that melts and flows out of the glass
The glass itself, which makes water when cold

explain.why: Glass has no holes for water to pass through.
The glass is not leaking.
A glass cannot make water.

solution: Water vapour in the air touches the cold glass and condenses.

items.stem: A puddle on a concrete floor slowly disappears on a sunny day. What has happened to the water?
options: It has changed into water vapour in the air
It has frozen into a thin sheet of ice on the floor
It has soaked down into the concrete floor
It has been used up and is gone for good

explain.why: The Sun makes things warm, so ice would not form.
Concrete floors do not soak up this much water.
Water does not disappear. It changes state.

solution: The water gains heat from the Sun and evaporates.

items.stem: A kettle of water is boiling. What is the white mist at Y made of?
options: Water vapour coming out of the spout

explain.why: Water vapour is a gas that we cannot see.
The kettle only contains water.
The air above a kettle is too hot for ice.

solution: Water vapour cools in the air and condenses into tiny drops, which we see as mist.

25 °C is below the melting point of S, so S is solid.

solution: A liquid is above its melting point and below its boiling point. 25 °C is between -20 °C and 80 °C.

items.stem: Ice at -5 °C is heated in a beaker. What is the first change seen when the ice reaches 0 °C?
options: The ice turns into water vapour

explain.why: Boiling happens much later, at 100 °C.
Heating cannot make water freeze.
Ice becomes liquid first.

solution: At 0 °C the ice starts to melt.

items.stem: Which states of water can flow?
options: Ice, which can be poured out
Water vapour only, since it spreads out

explain.why: Ice keeps its shape and does not flow.
Ice does not flow.
Liquid water can flow too.

solution: Liquids and gases can flow, but solids cannot.

items.stem: Water in an ice tray is put in a freezer and turns into ice. What happens to the water?

explain.why: Water must lose heat to freeze.
Melting is ice becoming water.
The water is becoming ice, not melting.

solution: Water gives out heat to the cold freezer and becomes ice.

items.stem: A bathroom mirror becomes misty after a hot shower. Which change caused this?
options: Water on the mirror freezing into ice
Water vapour condensing on the cool mirror
Water vapour boiling away on the mirror
Hot water melting on the mirror

explain.why: The mirror is not cold enough to make ice.
Boiling needs the water to gain heat.
Melting is ice turning into water.

solution: Water vapour from the shower loses heat to the cool mirror and condenses into tiny droplets.

items.stem: Which state of water can be squeezed into a smaller space most easily?

explain.why: A solid is hard to squeeze smaller.
A liquid is hard to squeeze smaller.
Neither can be squeezed easily.

solution: A gas can be squeezed into a smaller space.

items.stem: The water in a beaker is bubbling and the thermometer reading is shown. What does the reading tell us?
options: The water is not yet hot enough to boil

explain.why: Ice melts at 0 °C.
Water freezes at 0 °C.
The reading is at the boiling point.

solution: The reading is 100 °C, the boiling point of water.

explain.why: 100 °C is above the boiling point of P, so P is a gas.
100 °C is below the melting point of R, so R is a solid.
100 °C is above the boiling point of S, so S is a gas.

solution: 100 °C is between -39 °C and 357 °C, so Q is a liquid.

items.stem: A block of ice at 0 °C is placed in a warm room. What happens to the temperature of the ice while it is melting?
options: It rises steadily as the room is warm
It falls below 0 °C as the ice loses cold
It stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted

explain.why: The temperature stays at the melting point until the ice is gone.
The ice gains heat from the room. It does not get colder.
Only boiling water reaches 100 °C.

solution: The heat gained is used to melt the ice, so the temperature stays at 0 °C.

items.stem: Water in an open beaker is boiling on a stove. The thermometer stays at 100 °C even though the flame is still on. What is the heat being used for?
options: Changing liquid water into water vapour
Turning water vapour back into liquid water

explain.why: The reading is not rising.
That change gives out heat.
The heat is used to change the water's state.

solution: The heat is used to change water into water vapour, not to raise the temperature.

items.stem: On a cool morning the inside of a bus window is covered with tiny drops. What are the drops?
options: Liquid water formed from water vapour in the passengers' breath
Ice that has melted from the window glass
Water vapour that has become visible
Water that has leaked through the glass from outside

explain.why: The glass is not made of ice.
Water vapour cannot be seen. The drops are liquid.
The drops form on the inside, from the warm moist air.

solution: Water vapour from breath cools on the cold glass and condenses into liquid drops.

items.stem: Which statement about boiling and evaporation is correct?
options: Boiling happens only at the surface, but evaporation happens throughout the water
Both happen only when water is at 100 °C
Evaporation needs the water to lose heat
Evaporation happens only at the surface, but boiling happens throughout the water

explain.why: Bubbles form inside boiling water.
Evaporation also happens at lower temperatures.
Both changes need heat to be gained.

solution: Evaporation takes place at the surface at any temperature. Boiling takes place throughout the liquid at 100 °C.

items.stem: The table describes water in three forms X, Y and Z. Which one is water vapour?

explain.why: X has a fixed shape and a fixed volume, so it is ice.
Y takes any shape but keeps its volume, so it is liquid water.
Neither of them spreads out to fill a space.

solution: Water vapour has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.

items.stem: Which of the following changes needs water to lose heat?
options: A wet floor drying in the hot Sun
Water vapour forming drops on a cold window
An ice cube turning into water in a cup
Water bubbling away in a hot pot

explain.why: Drying means water gains heat and evaporates.
Melting needs heat to be gained.
Boiling needs heat to be gained.

solution: Condensation is the only change here in which water loses heat.

items.stem: Which of the following describes boiling?
options: Liquid water changes to water vapour throughout the liquid at 100 °C
Ice changes to liquid water throughout the block at 100 °C
Water vapour changes to liquid water on cooling at 100 °C
Liquid water changes to ice throughout the liquid at 0 °C

explain.why: That describes melting, which happens at 0 °C.
That is condensation.
That is freezing.

solution: Boiling is the change from liquid to gas, happening in the whole liquid at 100 °C.

items.stem: A beaker of water at 15 °C is put in a freezer. The thermometer shows the same reading for a long time while the water turns into ice. What is the reading?

explain.why: That is the freezer's temperature, reached only after all the water has frozen.
The water has cooled well below its starting temperature.
That is the boiling point.

solution: Water freezes at 0 °C, and its temperature stays there until all of it is ice.

items.stem: A student pours 200 mL of water from a jug into a tall glass, and then into a wide bowl. Which statement is correct?
options: Both the shape and the volume of the water change
The shape of the water stays the same but its volume changes
The shape of the water changes but its volume stays at 200 mL
Neither the shape nor the volume of the water changes

explain.why: The amount of water stays the same.
Liquid water takes the shape of its container.
The shape follows the container.

solution: A liquid takes the shape of its container and keeps its volume.

items.stem: On a hot day an ice lolly melts and drips. What happens to heat?
options: The lolly loses heat to the air
The lolly gains heat from the air
The air gains heat from the lolly
No heat moves, since the lolly is cold

explain.why: Melting needs heat to be gained.
Heat flows from the hot air to the cold lolly.
A difference in temperature always makes heat flow.

solution: Heat flows from the warm air to the cold lolly, which melts.

items.stem: The temperature at which pure liquid water changes into a gas is called the ____ point.

explain.why: Melting is the change from solid to liquid.
Freezing is the change from liquid to solid.
Condensation is the change from gas to liquid.

solution: Water changes to a gas at its boiling point, 100 °C.

items.stem: Ice cubes at 0 °C are put into hot tea at 80 °C and the tea is stirred until all the ice has melted. Which describes the final temperature of the tea?
options: Exactly 0 °C, the same as the ice

explain.why: There was much more heat in the hot tea than the ice needed.
The tea loses some heat to the ice, so it cools.
The tea cannot become hotter by adding ice.

solution: The tea loses heat to the ice, which melts and warms up, so the final temperature is between 0 °C and 80 °C.

items.stem: Mei Ling wants to find out how the mass of ice affects the time it takes to melt in a warm room. Which is the measured variable?
options: The time taken for the ice to melt
The mass of ice put in each beaker
The temperature of the warm room
The type of container that is used

explain.why: This is the variable she changes on purpose.
This should be kept the same.
This should be kept the same.

solution: She changes the mass and measures the time taken.

items.stem: A beaker of crushed ice and water is left on a warm table. The thermometer in the beaker is read every minute while some ice is still left. What does it show?
options: A reading that slowly rises above 0 °C
A reading that rises to the room temperature at once
A reading of 0 °C all the time

explain.why: Heat from the room melts the ice instead of warming it.
The ice is gaining heat, not losing it.
While ice remains, the mixture stays at 0 °C.

solution: The heat gained is used to melt ice, so the temperature stays at 0 °C until the ice is gone.

items.stem: More droplets form on the outside of a cold can on a very humid day than on a dry day. Why?
options: The air is hotter and gives more heat to the can
The can makes more water from the cold
The air has more water vapour that can condense
More ice melts inside the can

explain.why: Heat gained by the can does not make droplets.
A can cannot make water.
The droplets come from outside the can.

solution: More water vapour in the air means more of it condenses on the cold can.

items.stem: A girl walks from an air-conditioned room into the warm, humid air outside. Her spectacles become covered with a fine mist. Why?
options: Water vapour in her breath freezes on the lenses
Water vapour in the warm air condenses on the cold lenses
The lenses make water when they warm up
Water inside the lenses boils away to the surface

explain.why: The lenses are cold, but not below 0 °C.
Glass cannot make water.
Glass does not contain water.

solution: The lenses are cooler than the air, so water vapour touching them loses heat and condenses.

items.stem: Two cans in a 30 °C room each hold water. Can A has iced water. Can B has water at 30 °C. Droplets form only on Can A. Why?
options: The surface of A is cold enough to make water vapour lose heat
Can B has no water vapour in the air around it
Can A gives out more heat to the room than Can B does
The water in Can B has already evaporated and boiled away

explain.why: Both cans are surrounded by the same air.
Can A is colder, so it gains heat.
Water at 30 °C does not boil.

solution: Only the cold surface cools the nearby air enough for water vapour to condense.

items.stem: A sealed bottle of iced water is weighed before and after droplets form on its outside. The total mass has gone up. What does this show?
options: The water in the droplets came from inside the bottle
The ice in the bottle melted into the droplets
The ice in the bottle became heavier as it got colder
The water in the droplets came from the air

explain.why: The mass would not go up if water only moved from inside the bottle.
The bottle is sealed, so melting ice stays inside.
Water drops have mass.

solution: Extra mass can only come from outside the sealed bottle, so the droplets came from water vapour in the air.

items.stem: Aisha wants to find out whether the starting temperature of the water affects how fast an ice cube melts. Which set-up is a fair test?
options: Two beakers of water at 20 °C and 40 °C, with one ice cube and one crushed ice
A beaker of 100 mL of water at 20 °C and a beaker of 200 mL of water at 40 °C
Two beakers of 100 mL of water at 20 °C and 40 °C, each with an identical ice cube
One beaker of water at 20 °C tested for a long time and another tested for a short time

explain.why: The ice differs, so more than one thing changes.
The amount of water also changes.
The time is not the thing to be changed.

solution: Only the starting temperature of the water is changed.

items.stem: Which of the following is true for ice, liquid water and water vapour?
options: They all keep their own shape in any container
They all have mass and take up space
They all can flow from one container to another
They all have a fixed volume that never changes

explain.why: Only ice keeps its own shape.
Ice does not flow.
Water vapour spreads out to fill its container.

solution: All three are matter, so they have mass and take up space.

items.stem: A tube of each substance is placed in a water bath at 100 °C. Which substance that is a liquid at 20 °C will boil?

explain.why: Q boils at 357 °C, far above 100 °C.
R is a solid at 20 °C and boils at 2750 °C.
S is already a gas at 20 °C, so it is not a liquid.

solution: Only P is a liquid at 20 °C with a boiling point (78 °C) below 100 °C.

-100 °C is below the melting point of R, so R is solid.
-100 °C is above the boiling point of S, so S is a gas.

solution: -100 °C is between -115 °C and 78 °C, so P is a liquid.

It rises steadily to room temperature

It has a fixed volume like liquid water

Water vapour is a gas.
A gas spreads out to fill the space it is in.

solution: Water vapour is an invisible gas that is always in the air.
